The octet rule states that atoms tend to lose electrons (i.e. undergo oxidation), 
gain electrons (i.e. undergo reduction) or share electrons in order toachieve the 
eight-electron configuration of a noble gas. However, there are exceptions to 
the octet rule. Some elements of groups 2 and 13 may form stable compounds 
with less than eight electrons (incomplete octet) in their valence shell while most 
elements of the third and following periods can have more than eight electrons 
(expanded octet) around their atoms. 
Lewis formulas, also known as electron dot or Lewis structures, show all valence 
electrons (bonding and non-bonding pairs) in a malecule or palyatomic ion. 
Figure 2 shows how a fluorine molecule, F,, is formed from two fluorine atoms. 
Each atom contributes one electron to the shared electron pair in order to 
achieve a stable eight-electron configuration (full octet). 
More than one pair of electrons can be shared, as, for example, in the 
oxygen molecule (figure 3). A double bond, like the one in the oxygen 
molecule, is stronger and shorter than a single bond between the same 
atoms, and a triple bond (for example, in Nz) is stronger and shorter than a 
double bond. 
Each pair of electrons in a Lewis formula can be represented by two dots 
(*+), two crosses (xx) or a line (—). In figure 4, shared pairs of electrons (the 
bonding pairs) are shown as lines, and the lone pairs are shown as pairs 
of dots. The central atom in each of these species has four electron pairs 
(shared and lone), giving a total of eight electrons and thereby obeying the 
octet rule.

Shapes of molecules and the VSEPR model 
Lewis formulas do not represent three-dimensional shapes of molecules and 
ions. These shapes can be deduced using the valence shell electron pair 
repulsion (VSEPR) model. The basic rules of the VSEPR model are: 
* electron domains are regions of increased electron density, such as 
bonding or lone electron pairs 
¢ double and triple bonds count as one electron domain each 
* electron pairs repel one another to be as far apart as possible in space 
* lone pairs have a greater repulsive effect than bonding pairs. 
The electron domain geometry is the arrangement of both bonding pairs and 
lone pairs on the central atom. The molecular geometry is the actual shape of 
the molecule, which takes into account the arrangement of bonding pairs only. 
For example, ammonia, NH,, has four electron domains and thus a tetrahedral 
electron domain geometry, but its molecular geometry of the three covalent 
bonds is trigonal pyramidal. Molecular geometries based on two, three and 
four electron domains are shown in table 3. 
Lone pairs of electrons occupy more space than bonding pairs, so the 
repulsion between electron pairs decreases as follows: 
lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair—bonding pair 
Thus, the presence of lone pairs reduces bond angles: for example, in water, 
H,0, an AB,E, system (with A representing the central atom, B a bonding pair 
and E a lone pair), the bond angle is reduced from the ideal tetrahedral value

2.2 The covalent model 
Like any other theory, the VSEPR model has its limitations. For example, it 
is unable to predict exact bond angles in molecules or ions, and it cannot 
be used to deduce the three-dimensional structures of species containing 
transition elements with incomplete d-sublevels. Nevertheless, this model 
correctly predicts the spatial arrangement of covalent bonds in many 
molecular species and explains the observed deviations of bond angles 
from their ideal values. 
Polar covalent bonds and electronegativity, x 
Some covalent molecules contain polar covalent bonds, in which the shared 
electrons spend more time closer to one nucleus than the other. As a result, 
one atom carries a partial positive charge, &*, and the other a partial negative 
charge, &, for example, H*—F*. Such bonds are intermediate between 
non-polar covalent and ionic. 
Bond polarity can be characterized by the difference in electronegativity (Ay) 
values of the bonded atoms. Electronegativity ranges from 0.8 for heavy alkali 
metals to 4.0 for fluorine, the lightest halogen. The larger the difference in 
electronegativity, the greater the polarity of the bond (table 5).

Polar molecules 
The polarity of individual bonds and the shape of a molecule can be used 
to predict whether or not the molecule as a whole is polar. For example, in 
carbon dioxide, COZ, the two C=0 bonds are polar (Ax = 0.8). However, this 
molecule is symmetrical and linear, and the two dipoles of C=0 bonds have 
equal magnitudes and point in opposite directions, so they cancel each other 
out. As aresult, CO, is a non-polar molecule. In contrast, carbonyl sulfide, 
OCS, also a linear molecule, is polar because the two bond dipoles have 
different magnitudes and therefore do not cancel each other out. Another 
example is the SBI‘2 molecule with two polar S—Br bonds (Ax =0.4). Since 
SBr, is a bent molecule, the dipoles of the two bonds do not cancel each 
other out, so the molecule itself is also polar.

Covalent network compounds have high melting points because the strong 
covalent bonds must be broken before melting occurs. For the same reason, 
most covalent network compounds are brittle, as atoms in their structures 
cannot move past one another without breaking the covalent bonds. 
Intermolecular forces of attraction 
The bulk physical properties of molecular substances result from the different 
types of forces of attraction between their molecules. 
In order of increasing relative strength, intermolecular forces of attraction 
are London (dispersion) forces < dipole-dipole forces < hydregen bonding, 
assuming that the molar masses of interacting molecules are similar. 
London (dispersion) forces and dipole—dipole forces are both van der Waals 
forces, which are weak electrostatic attractions between molecules.

London (dispersion) forces 
London (dispersion) forces depend on the number of electrons and the size of 
the electron cloud; the larger the cloud and the further the valence electrons 
are from the nucleus, the more easily the electron cloud can be polarized 
(distorted by an external electric field). In addition, a long molecule with a 
large surface area will experience stronger London forces than a spherical 
molecule with a small surface area. 
Dipole—dipole forces 
Dipole—dipaole forces occur between polar molecules with a permanent (not 
instantaneous) dipole moment. An attraction between the positive end of one 
permanent dipole and the negative end of another permanent dipole keep 
adjacent polar molecules together. 
Dipole-induced dipole forces 
Dipole-induced dipole forces occur between polar molecules, which have a 
permanent dipole, and non-polar species. The proximity of a polar molecule 
induces a temporary dipole on the adjacent non-polar species. This results in a 
net force of attraction between the two species. 
Hydrogen bonding 
The strongest intermolecular force, hydrogen bonding, occurs between 
molecules containing an F—H, O—H or N—H bond. These bonds are 
polar, and the larger atom has a lone pair of electrons. That lone pair is 
attracted to the hydrogen atom with a partial positive charge, thus forming 
a hydrogen bond (figure 8). Hydrogen bonding can also be intramolecular, 
in which case an O-H or N-H group interacts with an N, O or F atom of the 
same molecule.

Identify the intermolecular forces of attraction present in Ne, CH_F, and

Example 6 
Comment, with reference to intermolecular forces, on 
the fact that the boiling point of carbon tetrachloride, 
CCl,, is 76.72°C, whereas the boiling point of 
fluoromethane, CH,F, is -78.2°C. 
Solution 
* You first need to work out the types of 
intermolecular forces of attraction present in each 
compound. 
* CCl,: only London (dispersion) forces are present, 
as CCl, is a non-polar molecule. 
CH,F: has both London (dispersion) forces and 
dipole-dipole forces, since CH,F is a polar 
molecule. 
The additional intermolecular force of attraction 
in CH,F might suggest that the boiling point of 
this compound should be higher than that of 
CCl,. However, this is only true for species with 
similar molar masses. The molar mass of CCl, 
(153.81 gmol™) is significantly higher than that of 
CH,F (34.04 gmol™), so the number of electrons 
and thus the polarizability of the electron cloud in 
CCl, are also higher. As a result, the greater London 
(dispersion) forces of attraction in CCl, outweigh 
the additional dipole-dipole forces in CH,F, so 
CCl, boils at a higher temperature than CH,F.

Chromatography 
Chromatography is used to analyse and separate mixtures of substances. 
The separation is driven by the intermolecular forces between the mixture 
components and two substances (chromatographic phases) that differ 
in polarity. 
All chromatographic technigues follow the same basic principle: the 
components of a mixture are distributed between two phases, one of which 
(mobile phase) moves through another (stationary phase) in a certain direction. 
The mobile phase may be a liquid (in liquid chromatography) or a gas (in gas 
chromatography). The stationary phase can be a solid, a gel or a liquid on a 
solid support. The components of the mixture have different solubilities and/ 
or affinities for the two phases, so they move at different rates and therefore are 
separated (figure 9). 
The relative rates of movement of the components are characterized 
quantitatively by their retardation factors, R,. Components with high R, values 
have greater affinities to the mobile phase and thus move faster while the 
components with low R, values have greater affinities to the stationary phase and 
thus move slower. The unknown components of a mixture can be identified by 
comparing their R, values to those of standard samples or literature data. 
Chromatography terminology 
* Chromatography is an analytical technique that can be used to 
separate the components of a mixture, based on their relative 
attractions to mobile and stationary phases. 
* Paper chromatography (PC) uses paper as the stationary phase and 
an organic solvent (or mixture of solvents) as the mobile phase. 
* Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is similar to paper 
chromatography but it uses silica or other porous solid material 
spread on a metal or glass plate instead of paper. 
* The starting line in chromatography is a line on the stationary phase 
where the analysed mixture and standard samples are spotted. 
* Theretardation factor, R, is the ratio of the distance travelled by the 
centre of the spot to the distance travelled by the mobile phase:

Delocalization and resonance 
Some molecules or ions can be represented by two or more Lewis formulas, 
known as resonance structures, with different arrangements of covalent bonds 
and lone electron pairs. The “moving” bonds correspond to delocalized 
electrons that are shared between more than two atoms. 
* Resonance structures are the different Lewis structures for 
the same molecule orion in which a double bond can occupy 
different positions. The electrons of the “moving” double bond are 
delocalized over all the possible positions, which increases the 
stability of the species. 
* Delocalization is a quantum mechanical concept that describes 
1t bonding in a conjugated system, in which electrons are 
“smeared”, or “shared out” across more than two atoms. 
Each delocalized bond has a fractional bond order:

Species with expanded octets of valence electrons 
Some atoms can have more than eight electrons in their valence shell, which 
is known as the expanded octet. This is only possible for elements of the third 
and following periods because lighter elements do not have enough orbitals 
in their outer energy level to accommodate additional electron pairs. For 
example, the atom of nitrogen (n = 2) has only four valence orbitals (one 2s 
and three 2p), so it can hold up to four electron pairs in its valence shell. As a 
result, nitrogen cannot form any species with five or more covalent bonds, 
such as NF, or NF,". In contrast, the heavier analogue of nitrogen, phosphorus 
(n = 3) has eight valence orbitals (one 3s, three 3p and five 3d), so it can hold 
five or six electron pairs in its valence shell and form many stable species with 
an expanded octet of electrons, such as PF5 or PFG‘ (example 9).

Make sure that you understand the difference between the terms oxidation 
state (OS), formal charge (FC), ionic charge and partial charge. 
* Oxidation state (OS) is the apparent charge that an atom would have 
if the compound were composed of ions. The rules for deducing 
oxidation states are outlined in Structure 3.1. 
* Formal charge (FC) of an atom is the charge that the atom would have 
if all the elements present in the species had identical electronegativity 
values (y). 
* loniccharge is the actual charge of an ion (charged species) that 
results from the loss of electrons (oxidation) or the gain of electrons 
(reduction) by an atom or group of atoms. 
* A partial charge (represented by 8* or 87) is an actual charge with an 
absolute value of less than one elementary charge unit.

Hybridization 
A covalent bond is formed when atomic orbitals of two adjacent atoms overlap 
and merge into a molecular orbital containing two shared electrons. The 
valence shell of a carbon atom has one 2s and three 2p orbitals that contain a 
total of four electrons. In methane, CH,, the different atomic orbitals on carbon 
hybridize to form four identical hybrid orbitals, each with the same energy and 
with 25% s character and75% p character. These hybrid sp® orbitals can then 
form molecular orbitals with hydrogen atoms. 
Similarly, in ethene, H,C=CH,, each carbon atom has three sp? hybrid orbitals 
and one p orbital. The hybrid orbitals of each C atom form three @ bonds 
(two with H atoms and one with the other C atom) while the p orbitals of the 
two C atoms overlap sideways to form the it bond. In ethyne, HC=CH, each 
carbon atom has two sp hybrid orbitals and two p atomic orbitals.
